To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
health professionals have mixed attitudes towards developmental screening tools, with a lack of knowledge and time being the most commonly cited barriers to using them.

health professional perceptions regarding screening of developmental surveillance for children are varied and influenced by the tools used and by the health professional’s understanding of developmental milestones.

health professional attitudes, enabler and barriers to developmental surveillance practices, including screening tools, are influenced by their perception of the parents’ knowledge of their child’s developmental status.
In summary, our research is concerned with
improving early child development and health outcomes for children in the South West Sydney region.
the identification of barriers to the uptake of recommended developmental screening tools in the primary health care setting and how these barriers can be overcome.
improving early identification of developmental delays in the South Western region of Sydney.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of screening tools is not a simple task and that there are several barriers and enablers that need to be taken into consideration when planning and implementing developmental surveillance programs.
there is a need for a comprehensive and integrated developmental surveillance system in Australia, and that the PEDS and the ASQs are not the only options available to achieve this.

there is a need for more research to determine the most effective integrated model of care which would allow for better collaboration between parents, service providers and health professionals, as well as improved information sharing between different health professionals involved in the screening and surveillance programs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current screening tools, PEDS and ASQS have been used by CFHNs and are well received by the parents.
there are a range of barriers and enablers to the uptake of screening tools and surveillance in general and these are different for the various health professionals and their patients.
the use of these screening tools is limited due to a range of barriers including lack of time and training, and the lack of a coordinated approach to surveillance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of the PEDS and the ASQs is not optimal and there is a need for better integration of developmental surveillance into the primary care system.

there is a need for a more comprehensive approach to the developmental screening process that will allow for a greater awareness and understanding of developmental screening and surveillance tools amongst all health care professionals.
the current surveillance tools are not being used to the best of their potential.
